title: “THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE”—BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING FIRST THAT MOST PEOPLE DON’T WANT TO HEAR
paragraphs: “THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE”—BUT JESUS SAID SOMETHING FIRST THAT MOST PEOPLE DON’T WANT TO HEAR

Before Jesus promised freedom, He exposed a slavery that can exist behind a smile, inside a church, and even in the heart of someone who believes they are already free. The forgotten conversation in John 8 may change how you understand sin, repentance, grace, and the freedom only Christ can give.
There is a kind of prison where the doors are open, but the prisoner never leaves.
No chains around the wrists. No guards standing outside. No iron bars blocking the sunlight.
Just a person who keeps promising, “This is the last time.”
The last time they will open that website.
The last time they will surrender to that temptation.
The last time they will lie to someone who trusts them.
The last time they will let bitterness poison their heart.
The last time they will return to something they know is destroying them.
And for a little while, they mean it.
They pray. They cry. They feel ashamed. They promise God they will change.
Then something happens.
A lonely night. An unexpected disappointment. An argument. A memory. A moment when nobody is watching.
And suddenly, they are standing in the same place again.
Doing the very thing they swore they would never do.
Perhaps you know that place.
Perhaps you have stood there more times than you want to admit.
And perhaps the most frightening part is not that you keep falling.
It is that you are beginning to wonder whether you will ever be free.
If that sounds painfully familiar, stay with this conversation Jesus had nearly two thousand years ago.
Because the words we love to quote about freedom were spoken in the middle of a confrontation about slavery.
And what Jesus said next was far more uncomfortable—and far more hopeful—than the inspirational quotation we usually see.
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” — John 8:32, KJV
Beautiful words.
Words printed on graduation banners, church walls, Christian merchandise, and countless social media posts.
But have you ever wondered what Jesus was actually talking about?
Freedom from what?
And why did the people listening to Him become so offended when He offered it?
The answer begins with a sentence that many of us would rather skip.
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.” — John 8:34, KJV
There it is.
The truth behind the promise.
Jesus was not merely offering people more information, better self-esteem, or freedom from difficult circumstances.
He was exposing something far deeper.
A slavery that could exist even in the life of someone who considered himself religious.
A slavery that could remain hidden beneath respectable behavior.
A slavery that could make a person defend the very thing that was destroying him.
And here is what makes this conversation so disturbing.
Jesus was speaking to people who believed they were already free.
John 8:31 tells us that Jesus addressed Jews who had believed Him.
He began by saying:
“If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” — John 8:31–32, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say that merely hearing a religious message automatically makes someone a genuine disciple.
He did not say that repeating a prayer removes the need to follow Him.
He did not say that truth is whatever makes a person feel comfortable.
He said, “If ye continue in my word.”
The original Greek is especially revealing.
ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ
Ean hymeis meinēte en tō logō tō emō.
“If you remain in my word.”
The verb μείνητε (meinēte) comes from μένω (menō), meaning to remain, abide, stay, or continue.
Jesus was describing something deeper than a moment of religious excitement.
He was describing a life that remains under His teaching.
A disciple does not merely admire the words of Jesus when they sound encouraging.
A disciple learns to remain with Jesus even when His words expose what needs to change.
That distinction matters.
Because it is possible to enjoy hearing about God's blessings while resisting His commands.
It is possible to love the idea of forgiveness while refusing to surrender a cherished sin.
It is possible to sing about freedom on Sunday and quietly return to captivity on Monday.
And Jesus loves us too much to call captivity freedom.
When He told His listeners that the truth would make them free, their response revealed something about the human heart.
They answered:
“We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free?” — John 8:33, KJV
Think about that.
They appealed to their ancestry.
Their religious identity.
Their connection to Abraham.
They could not understand why Jesus was speaking to them as though they needed liberation.
Their statement was especially striking given Israel's history of foreign domination and the Roman authority under which Judea lived.
But Jesus did not enter a political argument about their national history.
He went straight to the spiritual condition beneath their protest.
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
In Greek, the statement reads:
πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας
Pas ho poiōn tēn hamartian doulos estin tēs hamartias.
A close translation is:
“Everyone who practices sin is a slave of sin.”
The expression ὁ ποιῶν (ho poiōn) uses a present participle, describing someone characterized by doing or practicing sin.
That grammatical form contributes to the picture of sinful conduct, though the broader context must determine its full meaning.
Jesus was not teaching that a genuine Christian who commits a sin immediately loses salvation or becomes hopelessly enslaved again.
Scripture openly acknowledges that believers still struggle and must confess their sins.
First John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess their sins.
The issue is not whether a Christian has ever fallen.
The issue is whether sin is being defended, embraced, and allowed to rule.
There is a difference between fighting against sin and making peace with it.
Between falling into temptation and building a permanent home inside it.
Between grieving over disobedience and demanding that God approve it.
And only God knows the heart completely.
But Jesus gives us a warning worth taking seriously.
Sin does not remain a harmless visitor when we continually invite it to become our master.
It begins with a whisper.
“You deserve this.”
“Just one more time.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“God understands.”
And before long, the thing that once required a conscious decision begins to feel automatic.
What once troubled the conscience becomes easier to justify.
What once seemed unthinkable becomes familiar.
That is part of sin's terrible deception.
It promises freedom while demanding obedience.
It offers pleasure while concealing consequences.
It tells you that you are in control, even as your choices become increasingly difficult to resist.
And the enemy does not need to convince you that Jesus is nonexistent if he can persuade you to keep Jesus at a comfortable distance from the parts of your life you refuse to surrender.
Perhaps your struggle is not something obvious.
Perhaps it is pride.
The kind that makes every correction feel like an attack.
Perhaps it is envy.
The kind that makes another person's blessing feel like your personal failure.
Perhaps it is unforgiveness.
You can smile at people, serve in ministry, and quote Scripture while privately rehearsing the injuries you refuse to release.
Perhaps it is secret dishonesty.
The kind that has become so normal you barely recognize when you are doing it.
Or perhaps you are exhausted from a battle nobody else can see.
You love Jesus.
You believe His Word.
But you are ashamed of how often you return to the same temptation.
And somewhere inside, a terrible question keeps rising.
If I really belong to Christ, why am I still struggling?
Listen carefully.
The presence of a battle does not automatically mean the absence of faith.
But neither should the language of grace become an excuse to stop fighting.
The apostle Paul knew something about the agony of human weakness.
In Romans 7:19, he wrote:
“For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.”

Christians differ on precisely how Paul's experience in Romans 7 relates to life before and after conversion. But the passage unmistakably exposes the inability of human resolve, by itself, to overcome the power of sin.
And Paul does not end with self-confidence.
He cries:
“O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” — Romans 7:24, KJV
Notice the question.
Not, “What technique will finally make me impressive?”
Not, “How can I hide my weakness more effectively?”
Not even, “How can I save myself?”
Who shall deliver me?
The answer comes immediately.
“I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” — Romans 7:25, KJV
That is where freedom begins.
Not with pretending you have no problem.
Not with convincing everyone that your spiritual life is perfect.
Not with making another promise you cannot keep through willpower alone.
But with Jesus Christ.
The One who sees the sin you conceal.
The One who knows the shame you carry.
The One who understands the depth of human bondage.
And the One who came to save sinners.
This is why the conversation in John 8 becomes so extraordinary.
After exposing slavery, Jesus says something that changes everything.
“And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever. If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” — John 8:35–36, KJV
Read that again.
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
In Greek:
ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ, ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε
Ean oun ho huios hymas eleutherōsē, ontōs eleutheroi esesthe.
“If therefore the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”
The word ὄντως (ontōs) means truly, really, or indeed.
Not imaginary freedom.
Not merely the appearance of freedom.
Not the fragile freedom of someone who has simply managed to conceal a problem.
Freedom that comes from the Son Himself.
Jesus had moved from the image of slavery to the image of a household.
A slave did not possess the permanent standing of a son.
But the Son belongs in the house.
And the Son has the authority to liberate.
That is the breathtaking center of this passage.
Jesus does not merely identify the prison.
He declares Himself the One who can set the prisoner free.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere moral improvement.
Jesus did not come simply to tell sinners to behave better.
He came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins in His body on the cross, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The cross was not a demonstration that sin was unimportant.
It was a demonstration of how serious sin is—and how extraordinary God's love is.
God did not save us by pretending evil was harmless.
Christ bore the judgment our sins deserved.
And through His resurrection, He defeated death and opened the way to new life.
This is why forgiveness is not something we purchase with religious performance.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Grace is not God's permission to remain comfortable in sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires.
And Romans 6:14 declares:
“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.”
Notice the promise.
Not that believers will never experience temptation.
Not that spiritual growth will always be instant.
Not that every destructive habit will disappear without struggle, accountability, or wise help.
But that sin no longer has the rightful authority to reign over those who belong to Christ.
The Christian life is not a declaration that the battle is imaginary.
It is the announcement that sin is no longer our rightful master.
And because we belong to Jesus, we are called to resist it, confess it, turn from it, and walk by the Spirit.
Some victories come with remarkable suddenness.
Others unfold through painful, humbling seasons of repentance, prayer, renewed thinking, Christian fellowship, accountability, and perseverance.
For some struggles, seeking qualified professional help is also a wise part of pursuing healing and responsible care.
None of that makes Christ less sufficient as Savior.
It reminds us that sanctification is God's work in real human lives, not a performance designed to impress an audience.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this tonight.
You do not need to manufacture a testimony that sounds dramatic enough for people to applaud.
You need to come honestly to Jesus.
You do not need to pretend your wounds have already healed.
You need to stop treating those wounds as reasons to hide from the One who can restore you.
You do not need to convince God that you are worthy of His mercy.
You need to repent and trust the Savior who died for the unworthy.
Remember Peter?
The disciple who boldly declared his loyalty to Jesus.
The man who insisted he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
And then, under pressure, denied knowing his Lord three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
The sound of his own voice.
The realization that he had done the very thing he insisted he would never do.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that after the rooster crowed, the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
What a devastating moment.
A man who had walked with Jesus, heard His teaching, and witnessed His miracles had publicly denied Him.
But that was not the end of Peter's story.
After His resurrection, Jesus met His disciples again.
And in John 21, He addressed Peter personally, asking him about his love and entrusting him with the care of His sheep.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial had never happened.
He restored a fallen disciple and called him to serve.
That is grace.
Not the erasure of truth.
Not the celebration of sin.
But mercy that meets a repentant sinner and opens a future that failure seemed to have destroyed.
Peter's story does not mean every consequence of sin disappears.
It means that failure does not have to be the final chapter for someone who returns to Christ.
And that brings us to a question more personal than any theological argument.
What have you been calling freedom that has actually been keeping you in chains?
Maybe it is the freedom to do whatever you want.
But what if your desires have become your master?
Maybe it is the freedom to never forgive.
But what if the bitterness you protect is consuming your peace?
Maybe it is the freedom to keep a secret life.
But what if maintaining that secret has made genuine intimacy, honesty, and fellowship increasingly difficult?
Maybe it is the freedom to define right and wrong entirely for yourself.
But what if rejecting God's truth has left you increasingly unable to recognize what is destroying you?
Jesus did not say, “You will invent the truth, and your truth will set you free.”
He said that those who remain in His word will know the truth.
And later in the same Gospel, He declared:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6, KJV
Ultimately, Christian freedom is not separation from Jesus.
It is liberation through Jesus.
He is not simply a teacher who points toward freedom.
He is the Son who sets captives free.
And He calls us to follow Him in truth.
This is why repentance matters so deeply.
The Greek noun for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia), associated with a change of mind and, in biblical usage, a turning of one's life toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after getting caught.
It is not simply crying because sin has consequences.
It is a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in changed attitudes and actions.
It does not earn salvation.
It is part of the response of faith to the Gospel and belongs to the transformed life that God's grace produces.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
And perhaps the most dangerous thing a person can do is continually postpone that response.
“I will surrender when I am older.”
“I will forgive when they apologize.”
“I will stop when I am ready.”
“I will take my faith seriously when life settles down.”
But tomorrow is not promised.
And repeated resistance can harden the heart.
Hebrews 3:15 warns:
“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”
Today.
Not when you become impressive.
Not when your reputation is repaired.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Today, while His Word is confronting your heart.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you have been hiding a struggle, hear the invitation of Jesus.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Those are not the words of a Savior who enjoys humiliating broken people.
They are the words of the One who welcomes those who come to Him.
You can stop pretending.
You can confess what is true.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can ask for help.
You can begin making the difficult decisions that repentance requires.
And you can trust that the grace of Christ is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
If you have never placed your faith in Jesus Christ, you do not need to wait until you have cleaned up your life before coming to Him.
Come because you need a Savior.
If you already belong to Christ but have been living in compromise, do not use yesterday's profession of faith as an excuse to ignore today's call to repentance.
Return to His Word.
Confess your sin.
Seek the support of mature believers.
Make things right where possible.
And keep following Him.
Not because your obedience purchases His love.
But because His love is too precious to treat casually.
There is something deeply moving about the fact that Jesus used the language of slavery and sonship in the same conversation.
He knew what sin does.
He knew how human beings resist uncomfortable truth.
He knew how easily religious confidence can become a hiding place.
And still, He spoke of freedom.
He did not leave His listeners with the diagnosis alone.
He pointed them to the Son.
The One with authority to set them free.
The One who would soon stretch out His hands upon a Roman cross.
The One whose resurrection would proclaim that sin and death do not have the final word.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior will always return to this truth:
Not because Jesus calls evil good.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because grace makes repentance unnecessary.
But because the crucified and risen Christ can redeem sinners, restore the fallen, transform lives, and give hope where shame once seemed to have the final word.
And this is where I want to ask you something.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not to pressure you into revealing a private struggle to strangers.
But because someone else may need to know they are not the only person fighting to remain faithful.
You do not have to explain your private battle publicly.
God knows the details.

If someone comes to mind while you are reading this—a brother quietly struggling with temptation, a sister overwhelmed by guilt, a friend who has walked away from church, or someone who believes they are beyond forgiveness—consider sharing this article directly with them.
A simple share can carry Scripture into a home we may never enter, reach someone who would never search for a sermon, or begin a conversation about Jesus that might otherwise never happen.
Not because these words have power apart from Scripture, but because John 8:31–36 deserves more than a passing glance.
Return to the passage when temptation whispers that you cannot change.
Return when shame tells you to stay away from God.
Return when the world offers you a version of freedom that requires abandoning the truth.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, genuine encouragement, honest repentance, and the hope of Jesus Christ.
We also want to invite those who believe in this mission to help sustain and expand it.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing another inspirational post.
Our desire is to make Christ-centered teaching, devotional encouragement, and discipleship resources accessible to more people, including those who may not have the means to purchase them.
Behind every resource made available, every article prepared, and every effort to reach more readers is the practical reality that ongoing ministry requires time, work, and support.
Biblical giving is to be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we ask.
Not out of fear.
Not out of guilt.
Not with a promise that a financial contribution will purchase God's favor.
But as an opportunity for those who are able and willing to participate in work they believe is worth supporting.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, or meaningful gifts for someone you love.
It is the opportunity to help make the message of Jesus Christ more accessible.
You are just as welcome here.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
You can still help by praying, sharing the articles that speak to you, inviting others to follow, participating in meaningful conversations, and making use of the free biblical resources available.
We are grateful for every sincere expression of support.
Because the goal is not simply to build a larger audience.
It is to see people drawn toward the Savior.
To see Scripture opened and understood.
To see those trapped in secret shame discover the hope of forgiveness.
To see believers grow in holiness, love, humility, and obedience.
And to keep declaring that Jesus Christ is worthy of our trust, worship, and lives.
Before you leave, I want to bring you back to the words that started this entire conversation.
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
Those words are beautiful.
But do not separate them from the words that follow.
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
And above all, do not miss the glorious promise that completes the picture.
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
The truth Jesus proclaimed was never meant to be reduced to an inspirational slogan.
It confronts us.
It exposes us.
It dismantles the lies we use to protect our sins.
But in the hands of our Savior, truth is not the enemy of grace.
Truth shows us why we need grace.
And grace does not leave us where sin found us.
Perhaps you began reading this article believing that freedom meant nobody could tell you what to do.
Perhaps you have spent years insisting that everything is fine.
Perhaps you have learned how to look spiritually strong while carrying a private burden that is slowly exhausting you.
But maybe tonight, for the first time in a long time, you are willing to tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, I cannot save myself.”
“I have been defending what I should have confessed.”
“I have been hiding what You already see.”
“I need Your forgiveness.”
“I need Your help.”
“I need You.”
And there, in that place of honest surrender, you can begin again—not by trusting the strength of your promises, but by trusting the finished work and continuing grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest freedom is not the ability to sin without consequences.
It is belonging to the Savior who breaks sin's dominion and teaches His people to walk in newness of life.
The prison may have taught you to answer when sin called your name, but Jesus Christ is the Son who can set you free.
